opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think surgery is one of the most compelling places where robotics can genuinely help people, and it's a great example of augmentation rather than replacement. Surgeons are extraordinarily skilled, but they're also human. They get tired, their hands have a natural tremor, and some procedures require hours of very fine, repetitive motion. Suturing is a good example. It's tedious and it demands enormous precision, and the quality can vary from surgeon to surgeon, or even from the beginning of a long operation to the end.

What excites me is the idea that a robot could take over some of those subtasks, like tying a suture, retracting tissue, or holding a camera steady, under the supervision of the surgeon. The surgeon stays in charge of the judgment calls: what to cut, where, when to stop. The robot handles the parts where consistency and steadiness matter most. That's a partnership I find very appealing.

There's also a huge access issue. Many parts of the world don't have enough trained surgeons, and even in wealthy countries, outcomes depend a lot on who happens to be operating on you. If we can capture some of the skill of the very best surgeons and make it more broadly available, that could save a lot of lives and reduce complications.

I want to be careful not to overpromise, though. The body is enormously complex. Tissue is soft, it deforms, it bleeds, everyone's anatomy is a little different, and the cameras are often obscured. These are exactly the conditions where robots struggle. So I don't see robots doing autonomous surgery anytime soon. But I think we'll see gradual progress on specific, well-defined subtasks, with the surgeon always in the loop. That's where the real near-term value is, and it's a very exciting area of research.

r002.rationale: It describes a robot working under a surgeon’s supervision, but does not identify existing surgical robot assistants or clearly state that they are fully controlled by the human surgeon.

r003.rationale: It mentions suturing and consistency, but does not say robotic assistance would improve the evenness of the surgeon’s suturing.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should start by saying I'm actually fairly skeptical about a lot of the hype around robots. I've been working on robot grasping and manipulation for decades, and the honest truth is that robots are still remarkably clumsy. Picking up a cup off a cluttered table, something a toddler can do, remains surprisingly hard. So I don't go into this thinking robots are about to replace surgeons. That's not it at all.

What excites me is the idea of augmentation rather than automation. Surgery is one of the most demanding dexterous tasks humans do, and surgeons are extraordinary, but they're also human. They get tired. Their hands tremble slightly, especially late in a long procedure. They're working through tiny incisions, looking at a screen, manipulating instruments at awkward angles. And a lot of the time in surgery is actually spent on fairly repetitive subtasks: suturing, tying knots, cutting along a line, debridement, where you're removing dead tissue bit by bit. These are tedious, and they take up a lot of time where the surgeon's attention and skill could be used elsewhere.

So the question we've been asking in my lab, with the da Vinci systems and the work we've done with Intuitive Surgical and colleagues at UCSF and elsewhere, is whether we can get a robot to handle some of those subtasks under close supervision. Think of it like autopilot on an airplane. The pilot doesn't go away. They're still in command. But the system can take over the parts where precision and consistency matter more than judgment, and it can filter out tremor, scale down motions so a centimeter of hand movement becomes a millimeter at the instrument tip, and keep a steady hand for hour six exactly as it did in hour one.

And there's a learning component that I find really compelling. Every time a surgeon operates with one of these systems, there's data: the video, the instrument motions, the forces. There are millions of these procedures now. In principle, you can learn from the best surgeons in the world and make that skill available more broadly. That matters a lot when you think globally, where access to highly skilled surgeons is extremely uneven. If a robot can assist a less experienced surgeon in a rural hospital, or eventually help in settings where there's no surgeon nearby, that's a real difference in people's lives.

I'd also just say it's a wonderful research problem, because it forces you to be honest. Soft tissue deforms, it's slippery, it's occluded by blood, the lighting is terrible. You can't fake it in simulation and declare victory. If we can make progress in that environment, it tells us something genuine about robot dexterity. So it's exciting both because of the potential impact on patients and because it's one of the places where the gap between what robots can do and what we'd like them to do is most visible, and most worth closing.

r002.rationale: It says a robot may take over subtasks under close supervision, with the surgeon still in command; it does not describe existing assistants as fully controlled by the surgeon.

r003.rationale: It mentions robotic help with suturing and consistency, but does not clearly propose improving the evenness of a surgeon’s suturing.

astra-6.text:
Well, surgery is a great example of a setting where you don’t necessarily want to replace the human. You have a surgeon with extraordinary judgment and experience, and the question is: Can we give that person better tools? Can we help them move more precisely, reach places that are difficult to reach, and perform delicate maneuvers more reliably?

One way to do that is through motion scaling. The surgeon makes a relatively large, comfortable movement, and the robot translates that into a very small movement inside the body. You can also filter out tremor. So you’re preserving the surgeon’s control while extending what their hands can do.

What excites me is the possibility of taking that further, with assistance on particular subtasks. Think about handling a needle or placing a suture: The surgeon could guide the overall procedure while the robot helps execute a precise motion. That’s a very different challenge from asking a robot to perform an entire operation autonomously. And it gives us a way to develop useful capabilities incrementally, with the surgeon remaining central.

r002.rationale: It says current assistance preserves the surgeon’s control, with the surgeon guiding the procedure and remaining central.

r003.rationale: It mentions robot help with needle handling or suture placement, but does not propose improving the evenness of suturing.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is that a robot can act as an intermediary between the surgeon’s hands and the instruments. You can scale down the motion, so a relatively large movement of the hand becomes a very small, precise movement inside the patient. You can also filter out tremor. That gives a surgeon the possibility of working at a scale where our unaided hands are really quite limited.

And the interesting question is how we can extend that assistance. Could the robot help with a suture, or help keep an instrument from moving into tissue that the surgeon wants to avoid? The surgeon brings judgment and an understanding of what’s happening; the robot can contribute precision and consistency. That combination is what I find exciting.
